name: West Sikkim
meta_description: West Sikkim (Gyalshing district): Pelling, Yuksom, Pemayangtse, Khecheopalri and Goecha La. Real costs, routes, stays and the stories behind each place.
summary: West Sikkim, now Gyalshing district, is where the Sikkim kingdom was founded at Yuksom in 1642. Base yourself in Pelling (2,150 m) for Kangchenjunga views, Pemayangtse and the Rabdentse ruins, then go on to Yuksom, Khecheopalri Lake, Tashiding and the Goecha La trail. Plan 3–5 nights.
intro: West Sikkim is the part of the state where history sits closest to the surface. In 1642 three Tibetan lamas met at Yuksom and consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal on a stone throne at Norbugang. His son moved the court to Rabdentse, whose ruins lie in a forest below Pelling. Pemayangtse, the senior monastery of the Nyingma order in Sikkim, Dubdi, Sanga Choeling and Tashiding all belong to that first century of the kingdom.

Since the December 2021 reorganisation, the old West district has been split in two. The northern part is Gyalshing district, with its headquarters at Gyalshing, 10 km below Pelling. The southern part, around Soreng, Rinchenpong and Kaluk, became Soreng district. Travellers still say 'West Sikkim', and so do we, but on this site Rinchenpong, Kaluk, Hilley and Varsey sit under Soreng.

Pelling, at about 2,150 m, is the base most people use. On a clear morning between October and March it faces Kangchenjunga (8,586 m), Kabru and Pandim across the Rangeet valley. From Pelling, day trips reach Khecheopalri Lake, the Kanchenjunga Falls, Yuksom, Darap, Dentam, the Singshore Bridge and Uttarey on the Singalila Ridge by the Nepal border.

North of Yuksom lies Khangchendzonga National Park, which in 2016 became India's first UNESCO mixed World Heritage Site, listed for both its nature and its sacred meaning. The Dzongri and Goecha La trail starts in Yuksom. The district's people are mainly Limbu, Nepali, Lepcha and Bhutia, and homestays in Darap, Yuksom and Uttarey are the easiest way to meet them.

story.title: Three lamas, one throne and the first Chogyal
story.text: By the 1640s, Tibetan Buddhism was spreading south across the Himalaya, and three lamas of the Nyingma tradition, Lhatsun Chempo, Sempa Chempo and Rigzin Chempo, came into Sikkim from the north, west and south. According to Sikkim's own histories, summarised in Wikipedia's articles on Yuksom and Phuntsog Namgyal, they met at Yuksom, whose name is usually translated as 'meeting place of the three learned monks'. Needing a lay ruler to protect the faith, they went in search of Phuntsog Namgyal, a fifth-generation descendant of Khye Bumsa, a 13th-century prince from Kham in eastern Tibet, and found him near present-day Gangtok. In 1642, at the age of 38, he was consecrated as the first Chogyal, 'religious king', on a pine-covered hill at Norbugang. He was anointed with water from a sacred urn, and the four-seat stone throne where the lamas and the king sat still stands under a large tree. A chorten nearby is said to hold earth and water from across Sikkim. Yuksom served as the capital until 1670, when the second Chogyal, Tensung Namgyal, moved to Rabdentse near Pelling. The Namgyal dynasty ruled Sikkim until it joined India in 1975.
story.source: Wikipedia: Yuksom; Phuntsog Namgyal; Namgyal dynasty; Norbugang Chorten

little_known.fact: Rabdentse, Sikkim's second capital from 1670, lies in ruins below Pelling. Its stone throne, the Namphogang, was used for judicial pronouncements, and the Archaeological Survey of India protects the site as a monument of national importance.
Pemayangtse Monastery is by tradition reserved for ta-tshang, 'monks of pure lineage', who must be celibate and without physical deformity. It heads the Nyingma monasteries of Sikkim.
The Lepcha name for Khecheopalri Lake is Sho Dzo Sho, 'Oh Lady, sit here'. Birds are said to pick fallen leaves off its surface, and the lake has been protected by state notification since 2001.
Khangchendzonga National Park, established in 1977 and covering about 1,784 km², became India's first mixed (natural and cultural) UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2016.
The Limbu scholar Te-ongsi Sirijunga, who revived the Limbu script in the 18th century, was killed at Hee-Martam in West Sikkim around 1741, according to his Wikipedia biography.

highlights.title: Pemayangtse and the Rabdentse ruins
highlights.text: Walk from Pemayangtse, the senior Nyingma monastery of Sikkim at about 2,085 m, through forest to the ruins of Rabdentse, the royal capital from 1670. On the top floor of Pemayangtse sits the seven-tiered wooden model of Zangdok Palri, Guru Padmasambhava's heavenly palace, made by one lama.

highlights.title: Yuksom, where the kingdom began
highlights.text: See the stone throne at Norbugang where Phuntsog Namgyal was consecrated in 1642, the Kathok Lake whose water anointed him, and climb an hour to Dubdi, dated to 1701 and called the oldest monastery in Sikkim. Yuksom is also the gateway to Khangchendzonga National Park.

highlights.title: Khecheopalri, the sacred lake
highlights.text: A quiet lake at about 1,700 m in a forest bowl, sacred to Buddhists, Hindus and Lepcha. Walk the wooden jetty past prayer wheels, keep silent, and notice how few leaves float on the water. Stay in a village homestay to see it at dawn.

highlights.title: Tashiding and the Bumchu vase
highlights.text: On a heart-shaped hill between the Rathong Chu and Rangeet, Tashiding's chortens and carved mani stones host Bumchu each February or March, when lamas open a sacred vase and read the year's fortune in its water level.

highlights.title: Goecha La trail into the park
highlights.text: The trek from Yuksom through Sachen, Tshoka and Dzongri to Thansing and the Goecha La viewpoints faces Kangchenjunga's south-east side. Plan 8–10 days with a registered agency and guide; most groups turn back at View Point 1 at about 4,600 m.

highlights.title: Singshore Bridge and Uttarey
highlights.text: Cross the Singshore Bridge, about 240 m long and 100 m above the gorge, often called the highest in Sikkim, then climb to Uttarey at about 2,000 m on the Singalila Ridge for forest walks and quiet homestays near the Nepal border.

getting_there: Almost everyone reaches West Sikkim by road. From Bagdogra airport (IXB) or New Jalpaiguri (NJP) railway station, Pelling is about 135–145 km and 5–6 hours by private car via Sevoke, Melli, Jorethang, Legship and Gyalshing; indicatively ₹5,500–7,500 a car. Shared jeeps from Siliguri run to Gyalshing for about ₹500–650 a seat. From Gangtok it is about 115 km and 5–6 hours, via Singtam and Ravangla or Jorethang; shared jeeps cost about ₹350–500 to Gyalshing, and a private car ₹5,000–6,500. Pakyong Airport has had no scheduled flights since June 2024, and the Sevoke–Rangpo railway is not yet open. NH10 closes after monsoon slides; the alternative is via Darjeeling to Jorethang. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian travellers need no permit for Pelling, Yuksom, Khecheopalri, Tashiding or Uttarey. The Dzongri and Goecha La trek needs a Khangchendzonga National Park permit and fees, arranged at Yuksom through a registered trekking agency with a licensed guide. Foreign nationals need the Restricted Area Permit to enter Sikkim, applied for online via the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India, and a Protected Area Permit in a group of two or more for the Dzongri–Goecha La trek. Sikkim charges a ₹50 per tourist fee at check-in. Check current status before you travel.
money: On a budget, shared jeeps, a budget hotel in Pelling (₹1,500–3,000 a room) and homestays in Yuksom or Uttarey (₹1,200–2,200 per person with meals) keep a 3-night West Sikkim trip near ₹6,000–9,000 per person from Gangtok, plus a shared sightseeing car. At mid level, a private car for the circuit (₹3,500–5,000 a day) and a comfort hotel (₹5,000–11,000 a room) take it to roughly ₹18,000–30,000 per person for 3–4 nights. Premium stays such as The Elgin Mount Pandim run ₹12,000–22,000 a room. A Goecha La group trek costs about ₹15,000–30,000 per person for 8–10 days. All figures indicative.

months.summary: Cold, dry and often very clear. Kangchenjunga stands sharp at sunrise from Pelling's helipad and the Pemayangtse ridge, and rooms are cheaper than in autumn. Nights drop near freezing in Pelling and Uttarey, and snow can dust the Singalila Ridge. The Goecha La trail is snowbound and most agencies do not run it. A good month for monasteries, photography and quiet roads if you pack warm layers.
months.tip: Book a room with a heater or extra blankets, and plan sunrise from the helipad viewpoint.

months.summary: Still cold but bright, with the year's big religious dates. Pemayangtse holds its mask dances on the last two days of the Tibetan year, just before Losar, and Bumchu at Tashiding often falls in late February or early March. Mountain views stay good. Treks into Khangchendzonga National Park are mostly closed by snow until March.
months.tip: Festival dates follow the Tibetan calendar, so confirm them before booking.

months.weather: Pelling 5 to 17 °C, haze builds late in the month
months.summary: Spring starts. Rhododendrons begin flowering in the forests above Uttarey and on the Goecha La trail, magnolias appear on the Pelling ridges, and the first trekking groups leave Yuksom late in the month. Bumchu at Tashiding can fall in early March. Mornings are usually clear, afternoons hazier.
months.tip: Start sightseeing early; by afternoon haze often softens the mountain views.

months.summary: Rhododendron season peaks between about 2,500 m and 4,000 m, which makes April one of the best months for the Dzongri and Goecha La trek. Pelling is pleasant and green. Mountain views come and go with spring haze. School holidays have not yet started, so rooms are easier than in May.
months.tip: Book Goecha La treks 6–8 weeks ahead for April and May.

months.summary: Warm, green and busy with Indian family holidays. Pelling hotels fill and prices rise. Mornings can be clear, afternoons bring cloud and showers. The trekking season continues into the first half of the month. Waterfalls start to fill. A good month for families on the Pelling–Yuksom circuit.
months.tip: Reserve cars and rooms early for May; this is peak domestic season.

months.summary: The monsoon arrives in early to mid June. Roads to Yuksom, Uttarey and Gangtok see slides, leeches return to forest trails, and the mountains disappear behind cloud for days. Treks close. Hotels discount heavily. We only plan June trips for travellers who are flexible and happy with green hills and waterfalls instead of views.
months.tip: Keep a buffer day and check current status before you travel.

months.summary: Peak monsoon. The Kanchenjunga Falls and Rimbi run at full force, but NH10 and the Pelling roads are often blocked by slides. Mountain views are rare. Treks inside Khangchendzonga National Park are closed. Travel only with spare days and a flexible plan.
months.tip: NH10 closures are common; the alternative road is via Darjeeling to Jorethang.

months.summary: Still monsoon, with frequent rain and cloud. Fields around Darap and Hee Bermiok are deep green, and cardamom and paddy are growing, but slides and leeches make walking hard. Hotel rates are at their lowest. We suggest waiting for October unless your dates are fixed.
months.tip: Carry rain gear and leech socks if you walk any village trail.

months.summary: Rain eases through the month and the first clear mornings return in the second half. Roads are still repaired after the monsoon. Treks into the park usually reopen towards the end of the month or early October. Rooms are still discounted before the October rush.
months.tip: Late September can be a good-value window; check road status first.

months.summary: The best month for mountain views and the busiest. Kangchenjunga is visible most mornings, air is clear after the monsoon, and the Goecha La trail is at its best. Durga Puja and Diwali holidays fill Pelling, so book early. Village fields are being harvested around Darap and Uttarey.
months.tip: Book rooms and trek slots 6–8 weeks ahead for October.

months.summary: Excellent visibility, fewer crowds than October and colder nights. Treks run until early to mid November before snow closes the high passes. A fine month for photography, monasteries and village homestays, with sharp views of Kangchenjunga from Pelling, Uttarey and Hee Bermiok.
months.tip: Pack a down jacket for sunrise viewpoints and treks.

months.summary: Cold and clear, with some of the best mountain views of the year. Christmas and New Year weeks fill Pelling hotels, but the first half of the month is quiet and good value. Higher villages such as Uttarey may see frost or light snow. Treks into the park are mostly closed by snow.
months.tip: Book Christmas and New Year rooms by October.

faqs.q: Is West Sikkim the same as Gyalshing district?
faqs.a: Mostly. In December 2021 Sikkim reorganised from four districts to six. The old West Sikkim district was split into Gyalshing district (the north, with Pelling, Yuksom, Tashiding, Dentam and Uttarey) and Soreng district (the south, with Soreng, Rinchenpong, Kaluk, Hilley and Varsey). Travellers still say West Sikkim for both, and so do many drivers and hotels.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Plan 3–5 nights. Two nights in Pelling cover Pemayangtse, Rabdentse, Sanga Choeling and the Skywalk plus a day to Khecheopalri and Yuksom. A night in Yuksom adds Dubdi and Tashiding without rushing. Add a night in Uttarey or Darap for village life, or 8–10 days if you plan the Goecha La trek.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Pelling and West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Mid-October to mid-December gives the clearest views of Kangchenjunga, and March to May brings rhododendrons and pleasant weather. January and February are cold but often clear. June to September is monsoon: slides, leeches and cloud, though hotels are cheapest. Check current status before you travel in shoulder months.

faqs.q: How far is Pelling from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 115 km, or 5–6 hours by road, via Singtam and Ravangla or via Melli and Jorethang. A private car costs indicatively ₹5,000–6,500, and shared jeeps to Gyalshing about ₹350–500 a seat. NH10 between Gangtok and Singtam can close in the monsoon, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Pelling or Yuksom?
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit for Pelling, Yuksom, Khecheopalri or Tashiding. The Dzongri–Goecha La trek requires a Khangchendzonga National Park permit, arranged through a registered agency at Yuksom. Foreign nationals need the Restricted Area Permit for Sikkim, applied for online, and a Protected Area Permit for the trek. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see Kangchenjunga from Pelling?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days. Pelling faces Kangchenjunga (8,586 m), Kabru and Pandim across the Rangeet valley, and the helipad viewpoint in Upper Pelling and the Pemayangtse ridge give the widest views. The best odds are at sunrise from October to March. In the monsoon the range can stay hidden for weeks.

faqs.q: Is West Sikkim good for a family holiday?
faqs.a: Yes. The roads are long but the sights are gentle: monasteries, a sacred lake, waterfalls, the Skywalk and the Singshore Bridge, with short walks rather than hard hikes. Altitudes stay around 1,500–2,200 m, which suits children and seniors. Plan shorter driving days and avoid the monsoon months.

faqs.q: How much does a West Sikkim trip cost?
faqs.a: Indicatively, a budget 3-night trip from Gangtok with shared jeeps and budget rooms costs about ₹6,000–9,000 per person. A mid-range trip with a private car and good hotels runs ₹18,000–30,000 per person for 3–4 nights. Premium stays and private SUVs cost more. A Goecha La trek with an agency is about ₹15,000–30,000.

faqs.q: Can foreigners do the Goecha La trek?
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign nationals can trek to Dzongri and Goecha La with a Protected Area Permit, in a group of two or more, through a registered Sikkim trekking agency, in addition to the Restricted Area Permit for entering Sikkim, now applied for online. Rules change, so check current status before you travel and let us handle the paperwork.
